volume: 第八卷僧道部 Volume 8: Buddhist and Taoist Sects Department

stories.text: 一鄉官遊寺，問和尚：「吃葷否？」曰：「不甚吃，但逢飲酒時，略用些。」曰：「然則汝又飲酒乎？」曰：「不甚吃，但逢家岳妻舅來，略陪些。」鄉官怒曰：「汝又有妻，全不像出家人的戒行，明日當對縣官說，追你度牒。」僧曰：「不勞費心，三年前賊情事發，早已追去了。」
stories.translation: A local official visited a temple and asked the monk, "Do you eat meat?" The monk replied, "Not much, but when there is drinking, I use a little." The official said, "Then do you also drink alcohol?" The monk replied, "Not much; but when my father-in-law or mother's brother comes, I slightly accompany them with some." The local official angrily said, "You have a wife and completely do not follow the precepts of a monk. Tomorrow I will report to the county magistrate and reclaim your ordination certificate." The monk said, "You need not trouble yourself. Three years ago when the bandit case broke out, it had already been reclaimed long ago."

stories.text: 和尚做功德回，遇虎，懼甚，以鐃鈸一片擊之。復至，再投一片，亦如之。乃以經卷掠去，虎急走歸穴。穴中母虎問故，答曰：「適遇一和尚無禮，只擾得他兩片薄脆，就掠一本緣簿過來，不得不跑。
stories.translation: After a monk returned from performing meritorious deeds, he encountered a tiger and was very frightened. He struck it with one of his cymbals. When the tiger came again, he threw another piece; the result was the same. He then used a scripture scroll to drive it away, and the tiger hurriedly ran back into its den. The mother tiger in the den asked why, and it replied, "I just met an impolite monk. I only annoyed him with two thin cymbal pieces, so he took a scripture scroll over here. I had no choice but to run."

stories.text: 大族出喪，路逢大雨，女眷人等，避于路傍檐下。和尚沒處存身，暫躲開路神腹內。少頃，一僧從神腰裡伸頭探望，看雨住否。諸女眷驚曰：「我們回避，開路神要撒尿哩。」
stories.translation: A large family was holding a funeral when it encountered heavy rain on the way. The female relatives took shelter under an eave by the roadside. The monk had nowhere to take shelter and temporarily hid inside the belly of a road god statue. After a while, another monk stuck his head out from the waist of the deity to look and see if the rain had stopped. The female relatives were startled and said, "We should avoid it; the road god is about to urinate."

stories.text: 有素不信佛事者，死後坐罪甚重。乃傾其冥資，延請僧鬼作功果，遍覓不得。問人曰：「此間固無僧乎？」曰：「來是來得多，都發往酆都了。」
stories.translation: There was someone who had always disbelieved in Buddhist matters, and after death, he received a very severe punishment. He then spent all his spiritual wealth to invite monks and ghosts to perform meritorious deeds for him, but could not find any. He asked someone, "Are there really no monks here?" The person replied, "They do come in many numbers, but they have all been sent to Fengdu."

stories.text: 師父夜謂沙彌曰：「今宵可幹一素了。」沙彌曰：「何為素了？」僧曰：「不用唾者是也。」已而沙彌痛甚，叫曰：「師父，熬不得，快些開了葷罷。」
stories.translation: The master said to the novice at night, "Tonight we can have a vegetarian meal." The novice asked, "What does it mean by 'vegetarian'?" The monk said, "It means not using saliva." Soon the novice was in great pain and cried out, "Master, I can't endure it anymore. Quickly, let's resume eating meat."

stories.text: 一士借僧房讀書，忽聞鴉噪，連連叩齒。徒問：「相公為何？」答曰：「鴉噪。」徒曰：「我們丫燥，不是這等解法，是拓嚵吐的。」
stories.translation: A scholar borrowed a monk's room to study, when he suddenly heard crows squawking and kept clacking his teeth. His attendant asked, "Master, why are you doing this?" He replied, "Because of the crows' noise." The attendant said, "We say 'ya zao,' not interpreted this way; it means to chatter endlessly."

stories.text: 孝子懺悔亡父，僧誦普庵咒，至「南無佛佗耶」句，孝子喜曰：「正愁我爺難過奈何橋，多承佗過了。」乃出金勞之。僧曰：「若肯從重布施，連你娘等我也佗了過去吧」。
stories.translation: A filial son was performing repentance for his deceased father. A monk chanted the Puan spell, and when he reached the line "Namo Fote Ya," the filial son happily said, "I had just been worried that my father could not cross the Bridge of No Regrets; I am greatly relieved now that he has passed it." He then gave gold as a reward. The monk said, "If you are willing to make a generous offering, I will also help your mother cross over."

stories.text: 一僧追荐亡人，需銀三錢，包送西方。有婦超度其夫者，送以低銀。僧遂念往東方。婦不悅，以低銀對，即算補之，改念西方。婦哭曰：「我的天，只為幾分銀子，累你跑到東又跑到西，好不苦呀。」
stories.translation: A monk performed a memorial service for the deceased, requiring three qian of silver to escort them to the Western Paradise. A woman who wanted to transfer her husband's soul gave him low-quality silver. The monk then chanted for the soul to go eastward. The woman was displeased, presented more low-quality silver as compensation, and had it recalculated; then she changed the chanting to send him westward. The woman wept and said, "My heavens, just for a few coins of silver, you've had to run all the way east and then west. How hard it is!"

stories.text: 一僧患大氣脬，請醫治之。醫曰：「此症他人患之便可醫，惟你出家人最難治。」問何以故，答曰：「這個大脬內，都是徒弟們的屁在裡面。」
stories.translation: A monk suffered from a large gas pouch and invited a doctor to treat him. The doctor said, "This illness can be treated when others suffer from it, but for you monks, it is the hardest to cure." When asked why, he replied, "Inside this large pouch are all the farts of your disciples."

stories.text: 或問和尚曰：「汝輩出家人，修煉參禪，夜間獨宿，此物還硬否？」和尚曰：「幸喜一月止硬三次。」曰：「若如此大好？」和尚曰：「只是一件不妙，一硬就是十日。」
stories.translation: Someone asked a monk, "You monks who cultivate and meditate, when you sleep alone at night, does this thing still become hard?" The monk said, "Fortunately, it becomes hard only three times a month." He asked, "If so, isn't that very good?" The monk said, "Only one thing is not good: once it becomes hard, it lasts for ten days."

stories.text: 一人以幼子命犯孤宿，乃送出家，僧設酒款待。子偶撒一屁甚響，父不覺大慟。僧曰：「撒屁乃是常事，何以發悲？」父曰：「想我小兒此後要撒這個響屁，再不能夠了。」
stories.translation: A man, because his young son was said to have an ill-fated destiny due to a solitary star, sent him to become a monk. The monk set up wine to entertain and welcome him. The boy happened to let out a very loud fart, and the father could not help but grieve greatly. The monk said, "Passing gas is a common occurrence; why are you grieving?" The father replied, "I was thinking that my little son will no longer be able to pass such a loud fart from now on."

stories.text: 一僧每進房，輒閉門口呼「親肉心肝」不置。眾徒俟其出，啟鑰瞷之，無他物，帷席下一香囊耳。眾疑此有來歷，乃去香，實以雞糞。僧既歸，仍閉門取香囊，且嗅且喚曰：「親肉心肝呀，你怎麼這等，莫非撒了一屁麼？」
stories.translation: Every time a monk entered the room, he would shut the door and repeatedly call out "dear flesh and liver" without stopping. The disciples waited for him to leave, then opened the lock and peeped in. There was nothing else but a sachet under the mat and bedding. The disciples suspected there might be something unusual about it, so they removed the fragrance and filled it with chicken manure instead. After the monk returned, he still shut the door and took out the sachet, sniffing it while calling out, "Dear flesh and liver, how could you be like this? Did you pass a fart?"

stories.text: 頭虱為足虱邀飲，值其人行房事，致被阻，觀望久之方到。問：「何來遲？」曰：「不要說起。行至黑松林，遇一和尚甚奇，初時軟弱郎當，有似怯病和尚；已而昂藏堅挺，竟似少林和尚；及其出入不休，好像當家和尚；忽然嘔吐垂首，又像中酒和尚。」下虱曰：「究竟是甚和尚？」曰：「臨了背著袱包就走，還是個遊方和尚。」
stories.translation: Head lice were invited by foot lice for a drink, but when the man was engaged in sexual activity and thus blocked their way, they waited for a long time before arriving. They asked, "Why are you so late?" He said, "Don't even mention it." On the way to Black Pine Forest, we met a very strange monk. At first he was soft and drooping, like a sickly monk; then he became proud and firm, just like a Shaolin monk; when he kept going in and out without stopping, it looked like a head monk; suddenly he vomited and lowered his head, looking like a drunk monk." The foot lice asked, "So what kind of monk was it after all?" He said, "In the end, he just left with a bundle on his back; it turned out to be a wandering monk."

stories.text: 有買糞於寺者，道人索倍價。鄉人訝之，道人曰：「此糞與他處不同，盡是師父們樁實落的，泡開來一擔便有兩擔。」
stories.translation: There was someone who bought manure from a temple, and the Taoist demanded double the price. The villagers were surprised, and the Taoist said, "This manure is different from that elsewhere; it's all solidly dropped by the masters. When soaked, one basket becomes two baskets."

stories.text: 一秀才小便，和尚見之，大贊曰：「相公必然高中，生問：「何以知之？」僧曰：「適見龜頭有痣。相書曰：『龜頭有痣終鬚髮。』故以知之。」生曰：「你將來山門大興，妙不可言。」僧問：「何以見得？」答曰：「若要佛法興，除非僧贊僧。」
stories.translation: A scholar was urinating when a monk saw him and greatly praised, saying, "Master must certainly pass the imperial examination." The scholar asked, "How do you know this?" The monk said, "I just saw a mole on your turtle head." A physiognomy book says: "One with a mole on the turtle head will eventually grow beard and hair." Hence, I knew it." The scholar said, "Your temple will flourish greatly in the future; it is wonderful beyond words." The monk asked, "Why do you say so?" He replied, "If Buddhism is to flourish, monks must praise each other."

stories.text: 師號光明，徒號明光。客問：「賢師徒法號，如何分別？」徒答曰：「上頭光是家師，下頭光即是小僧。」
stories.translation: The master was named Guangming, and the disciple was named Mingguang. A guest asked, "How are your master-disciple dharma names distinguished?" The disciple replied, "The light on top is my master; the light below is this humble monk."

stories.text: 一婦遊虎丘，手持素扇。山上有賣字者，每字索錢一文，婦止帶有十八文求寫。賣字者題曰：「美貌一佳人，胭脂點嘴唇。好像觀音樣，少淨瓶。」子持扇，為館師見之，問：「此扇何來？」子述以故。師曰：「被他取笑了。」因取十七文，看他如何寫法。賣者即書云：「聰明一秀才，文章滾出來。一日宗師到，直呆。」生取扇含怒下山，途遇一僧，詢知其故。僧曰：「待小僧去難他。」遂攜十六文以往，寫者題曰：「伶俐一和尚，好像如來樣。睡到五更頭，硬（音上）。」僧曰：「尾韻不雅，補錢四文，求你換過。」賣字曰：「既寫，如何抹去？不若與你添上罷。」援筆寫曰：「硬到大天亮。」
stories.translation: A woman visited Tiger Hill, holding a plain fan in her hand. There was someone selling calligraphy on the mountain who charged one coin per character; the woman had only eighteen coins and asked for writing. The calligrapher wrote, "A beautiful lady, with rouge on her lips." "Looks like Guanyin, but without the vase." The woman held up her fan, which was seen by a tutor. The tutor asked, "Where did you get this fan?" She explained the reason to him. The tutor said, "You were teased by him." He then took seventeen coins and watched how he would write. The seller immediately wrote, "A smart scholar, whose essays flow out effortlessly." "One day the master arrived and just stood there dumbfounded." The scholar took the fan in anger and went down the mountain. On his way, he met a monk who asked about the reason. The monk said, "Let this humble monk go challenge him." He then took sixteen coins and went there. The writer inscribed: "A clever monk, resembling the Buddha himself." "Sleeping until the fifth watch of the night, hard (pronounced shang)." The monk said, "The ending rhyme is not elegant. Please give me four more coins and let me change it." The calligrapher said, "It has already been written; how can I erase it?" "It would be better to add something for you instead." He took up the brush and wrote: "Hard until daylight breaks."

stories.text: 有三人同行，途遇穿一破褲者。一友曰：「這好像獵戶張豝。」一人曰：「不然，還似漁翁撒網。」又一人曰：「都不確，依我看來，好像一座多年破廟。」問：「為何？」答曰：「前也看見和尚，後也看見和尚。」
stories.translation: Three people were traveling together, and on the way they met a man wearing a pair of torn pants. One friend said, "This looks like Hunter Zhang Ba." Another person said, "No, it still resembles a fisherman casting his net." Yet another person said, "Neither is correct. In my opinion, it looks like an old ruined temple." They asked, "Why?" The answer was given: "I saw a monk in front and also a monk behind."

stories.text: 秀才、道士、和尚三人，同船過渡。舟人解纜稍遲，眾怒罵曰：「狗骨頭，如何這等怠慢！」舟人忍氣渡眾下船，撐到河中，停篙問曰：「你們適纔罵我狗骨頭，汝秀才是甚骨頭，講得有理，饒汝性命，不然推下水去！」士曰：「我讀書人攀龍附風，自然是龍骨頭。」次問道士，乃曰：「我們出家人，仙風道骨，自然是神仙骨頭。」和尚無可說得，乃慌哀告曰：「乞求饒恕，我這禿子，從來是沒骨頭的。」
stories.translation: A scholar, a Taoist priest, and a monk were traveling together on the same boat. The boatman untied the mooring rope slightly late, and everyone angrily scolded him, saying, "Dog bone head, how could you be so slow!" The boatman endured the anger and ferried everyone ashore. After rowing to the middle of the river, he stopped his oar and asked, "You just called me a dog bone head earlier. What kind of bones are you, Mr. Scholar? If your explanation is reasonable, I will spare your life; otherwise, I'll throw you into the water!" The scholar said, "As a man of letters who follows the dragon and the wind, I am naturally a dragon bone head." Next he asked the Taoist priest, who said, "We monks and nuns have an air of immortals and Daoist bones; naturally we are immortal bone heads." The monk had no answer and in panic pleaded, "I beg for mercy. I am a bald monk who has never had any bones."

stories.text: 有浸苧麻于河埠者，被人竊去。適一婦人蹲倒滌衣，陰毛甚長，浸入河內，濯畢，帶水而歸。失苧者跟視水跡，疑是此婦偷去，罵詈不止。婦分辨不脫，怒將陰毛剪下，以火焚之。值鄰家方在尋雞聲喚，忽聞隔壁毛臭，亦冤是他盜吃了。兩邊喊罵，受屈愈深。婦思多因此物遺禍，將刀連陰戶挖出，拋在街心。值兩公差拘提人犯回來，踹著此物，仔細端詳，駭曰：「又是一樁人命了。怎麼和尚的下爬，被人割落在這裡。」
stories.translation: Someone who was soaking ramie in the river dock had it stolen by another person. At that moment, a woman was squatting to wash clothes; her pubic hair was very long and got immersed in the river. After washing, she went home with wet hair. The person who lost the ramie followed the water trail and suspected that this woman had stolen it, scolding her without end. The woman could not clear herself of suspicion and in anger cut off her pubic hair and burned it with fire. At that moment, a neighbor was just searching for his chicken and calling out its name when he suddenly smelled the burnt hair from next door and wrongly accused him of stealing and eating it. Both sides shouted curses, and their grievances deepened further. The woman thought that this object had brought her misfortune, so she used a knife to cut it out along with the genital area and threw it into the middle of the street. At that moment, two bailiffs who had just taken a criminal back were walking by and stepped on this object. They carefully examined it and exclaimed in horror, "This is another murder case." "How come the bald monk's lower part has been cut off and left here?"

stories.text: 一僧赴宴而歸，人問：「坐第幾席？」答曰：「首席是姓杜的，次席是姓徐的，杜徐之下，就是貧僧了。」
stories.translation: A monk returned from a banquet, and someone asked, "Which seat did you sit at?" He replied, "The first seat was for someone surnamed Du, the second seat for someone surnamed Xu. Below Master Du Xu is this humble monk."

stories.text: 一僧欲宿妓，苦無嫖錢，乃竊米一升而往。妓用大升量折，止存五合，嫌少不納。僧復往竊升米與之，方許行事。僧憤恨，乃以頭頂妓陰戶。妓曰：「差了。」僧曰：「你把大家伙處我，我亦把大家伙弄你。」
stories.translation: A monk wanted to stay with a prostitute but lacked money for the service, so he stole one sheng of rice and went there. The prostitute used a large measuring vessel to weigh it out, leaving only five ge, and found the amount too small, so she refused to accept him. The monk went back again and stole another sheng of rice for her, and only then was he allowed to proceed. The monk became furious and used his head to hit the prostitute's genital area. The prostitute said, "You're wrong." The monk replied, "You used your big thing to treat me, so I also used my big thing on you."

stories.text: 一僧宿娼，娼遽扳其頭以就陰。僧曰：「非也，此小僧頭耳。」娼意其嫌小，應曰：「盡夠了。」
stories.translation: A monk stayed with a prostitute, and the prostitute suddenly pulled his head toward her genital area. The monk said, "No, this is just my small monk's head." Thinking the monk was complaining about its size, the prostitute replied, "It's more than enough."

stories.text: 一士問僧云：「你看我腹中是甚麼？」僧曰：「相公自然滿腹文章在內。」士曰：「非也。」曰：「然則是五臟六腑乎？」士曰：「亦非也。」僧問何物，曰：「一肚皮和尚。若不信，現有一光頭，掛出在裡面。」
stories.translation: A scholar asked a monk, "What do you think is in my stomach?" The monk said, "Sir, your belly must naturally be full of essays." The scholar said, "No." He asked, "Then could it be the five zang and six fu organs?" The scholar said, "No, that is not it either." The monk asked what was in there. The scholar replied, "A belly full of monks." "If you don't believe me, there is a bald head hanging inside right now," he said.

stories.text: 老僧往後園出恭，誤被筍尖搠入臀眼，乃喚疼不止。小沙彌見之，合掌云：「阿彌陀佛，天報。」
stories.translation: An old monk went to the back garden to relieve himself but was accidentally pierced in the anus by a bamboo shoot tip and cried out in pain without stopping. A young novice saw this, clasped his hands together, and said, "Amituofo, heaven's retribution."

stories.text: 僧臨終，囑其徒曰：「享祀不須他物，只將你窟臀供座上足矣。」徒如命。方在祭獻，聽見有人叩門，忙應曰：「待我收拾了祭器就來。」
stories.translation: On his deathbed, the monk instructed his disciple, "For my memorial service, you need no other offerings; just place your arse on the altar and it will be sufficient." The disciple followed the order. While making the offering, he heard someone knocking on the door and hurriedly replied, "Wait a moment while I put away the sacrificial vessels."

stories.text: 僧見道家洗浴，先請師太，次師公，後師父，挨次而行，毫不紊亂。因感慨自嘆曰：「獨我僧家全無規矩，老和尚不曾下去，小和尚先脫得精光了。」
stories.translation: The monk saw that in the Daoist sect, when taking a bath, they first invited the elder nun, then the master grandfather, and finally the master father, proceeding in order without any confusion. He sighed and said with emotion, "Only in our Buddhist community is there no order at all. The old monks have not even undressed yet, but the young monks are already completely naked."

stories.text: 一僧與人對奕，因奪角不能成眼，躁甚頭癢。乃手摩頭頂而沉吟曰：「這個所在，有得一個眼便好。」
stories.translation: A monk was playing a game of Go with someone else. Because he could not form an eye by taking the corner, he became very agitated and itched on his head. He then rubbed his head and mused thoughtfully, "If there were an eye in this place, it would be perfect."

stories.text: 一秀才問僧人曰：「禿字如何寫？」僧曰：「不過秀才的尾巴彎過來就是了。」
stories.translation: A scholar asked a monk, "How is the character for 'bald' written?" The monk said, "It's nothing more than bending over the tail of the scholar's character."

stories.text: 一秀士每日往寺中聽講法，師問曰：「請教何謂『君子有九思』？」士答曰：「都在人身上：頭是三法司，耳是按察司，目是驗封司，鼻是通政司，口是縈膳司，肚是尚寶司，手是提舉司，足是行人司。」僧問：「還有一司？」生以手指陽物曰：「在這裡。」僧問：「何司？」答曰：「僧綱司。」
stories.translation: A young scholar went to the temple every day to listen to lectures. The master asked, "May I ask what is meant by 'a gentleman has nine thoughts'?" The scholar replied, "They are all on the human body: the head is the Sanfasi (Three Judicial Departments), the ears are Anchasī (Censorate Department), the eyes are Yanfengsi (Office of Verification and Enfeoffment), the nose is Tongzhengsi (Department of Communications and Administration), the mouth is Yingshansi (Office of Food and Supplies), the belly is Shangbaosi (Imperial Seal Office), the hands are Tijujsi (Supervisory Bureau), and the feet are Xingrensi (Bureau of Couriers)." The monk asked, "Is there still one more office?" The scholar pointed to his genital with his finger and said, "It's right here." The monk asked, "What office is it?" He replied, "It's the Senggangsi (Monastic Affairs Office)."

stories.text: 和尚途行，一小廝叫曰：「和尚和尚，光頭浪蕩。」僧怒云：「一個筋頭，翻在你娘肚上。」婦怒曰：「我家小廝，不過作耍，為何出此粗言？」僧曰：「娘娘，難道小僧當真，何須著急？」
stories.translation: A monk was walking on the road when a little boy shouted, "Monk! Monk! Bald head, you're wandering around." The monk angrily said, "With one somersault, I'll flip right onto your mother's belly." The woman angrily said, "My little boy was just playing around. Why did you say such a rude thing?" The monk replied, "Madam, if the young monk were serious, would I need to rush?"

stories.text: 一僧嫖院，以手摸妓前後，忽大叫曰：「奇哉，奇哉！前面的竟像尼姑，後面的宛似徒弟。」
stories.translation: A monk went to a brothel and touched the front and back of the prostitute. Suddenly, he shouted, "Extraordinary! Extraordinary!" "The front part resembles a nun, while the back is just like my disciple."

stories.title_en: Monk and Taoist arguing over a child
stories.text: 有僧道共偷一孀婦，有孕。及生子，僧道各爭是他骨血，久之不決。子長，人問之，答曰：「我是和尚生的。」道士怒曰：「怎見得？」子曰：「我在娘胎裡，只見和尚鑽進鑽出，並不曾見你道士。」
stories.translation: A monk and a Taoist had both secretly taken a widow, who became pregnant. When the child was born, the monk and the Taoist each claimed it as their own offspring, and they could not reach a decision for a long time. When the child grew up, someone asked him, and he replied, "I was born from the monk." The Taoist angrily said, "How can you be sure?" The child replied, "While I was in my mother's womb, I only saw the monk going in and out; I never saw you Taoist."

stories.text: 豬欄內忽產下一狗，事屬甚奇。鄰里環聚議曰：「道是（士）狗養的，又是豬的種，道是曰豬養的，又是狗的種。」
stories.translation: A dog was suddenly born in a pigpen, which was an extremely strange event. The neighbors gathered around and discussed, saying, "If it is the dog that was raised by (the scholar), then it is of pig stock; if it is said to be raised by the pig, then it is of dog stock."

stories.text: 一道士與婦人私，正行事，忽聞其夫叩門，道士慌甚，乃棄頭上冠子在床而去。夫既登床，摸著道冠問曰：「此是何物？」婦急應曰：「此是我褪下的屄殼。」
stories.translation: A Taoist had an affair with a woman. While they were engaged in the act, he suddenly heard her husband knocking on the door. The Taoist was very frightened and left his hat on the bed as he fled. After climbing onto the bed, the husband touched the Taoist's hat and asked, "What is this object?" The woman hurriedly replied, "This is my shed vulva shell."

stories.text: 有無妻者，每放手銃，則以瓦罐貯精。久之精滿，攜出傾潑，乃對罐哭曰：「我的兒呀，只為你沒娘，所以送你在罐裡。」
stories.translation: A man without a wife, whenever he discharged his firearm, would store the semen in a clay jar. After some time, when the semen was full, he took it out and poured it away. He then wept before the jar, saying, "My child, it is only because you have no mother that I had to send you into this jar."

stories.text: 一和尚偷婦人，為女夫追逐，既跳牆，復倒墜。見地下有光頭痕，遂捏拳印指痕在上，如冠子樣，曰：「不怕道士不來承認。」
stories.translation: A monk stole a woman and was chased by her husband. After jumping over the wall, he fell back down. Seeing a bald head mark on the ground, he then made a fist and pressed his finger marks onto it in the shape of a hat, saying, "The Taoist will not fail to come forward to claim this."

stories.text: 一道士自誇法術高強，撇得好驅蚊符。或請得以貼室中，至夜蚊蟲愈多。往咎道士，道士曰：「吾試往觀之。」見所貼符曰：「原來用得不如法耳。」問：「如何用法？」曰：「每夜趕好蚊蟲，須貼在帳子裡面。」
stories.translation: A Taoist boasted of his powerful magical abilities and had written an excellent mosquito-repelling talisman. Some people requested to obtain it and pasted it in their rooms, but at night the mosquitoes became even more numerous. They went to blame the Taoist, who said, "Let me go and take a look." Seeing the pasted talisman, he said, "It turns out you used it incorrectly." They asked, "What is the correct way to use it?" He said, "Every night after you have driven away the mosquitoes, you must paste it inside the mosquito net."

stories.text: 一道士過王府基，為鬼所迷，賴行人救之，扶以歸。道士曰：「感君相救，無物可酬，有避邪符一道，聊以奉謝。」
stories.translation: A Taoist passed by the site of a royal mansion and was bewitched by ghosts. He relied on passersby to rescue him, who supported him back home. The Taoist said, "I am grateful for your help; I have nothing to offer in return. There is one talisman for warding off evil spirits, which I will give you as a token of my thanks."

stories.text: 官命道士祈雨，久而不下，怪其身體不潔，褻瀆神明，以致如此。乃盡拘小道，禁之獄中，令其無可掏摸。越數日，獄卒稟曰：「老道士祈雨，小道士求晴，如何得有雨下？」官問何故，獄卒曰：「他在獄念道：『但願一世不下雨，省得我們夜夜去熬疼。』」
stories.translation: The official ordered a Taoist to pray for rain, but after a long time it still did not rain. They blamed the Taoist for his impure body and disrespectful behavior toward the deities, which had caused this situation. They then arrested all minor Taoists, confined them in prison, and ordered that they be kept from any opportunity to touch or manipulate things. After several days, the jailer reported, "The old Taoist prayed for rain while the young Taoists asked for clear weather. How can it possibly rain?" The official asked why this was so, and the jailer replied, "While in prison he recited: 'May it not rain for a lifetime, so we won't have to suffer pain night after night.'"

stories.text: 有尼姑同一妓者，死見閻工。王問妓曰：「汝前世作何生理？」妓曰：「養漢接客。」王判云：「養漢接人，方便孤身，發還陽世，早去超生。」問尼姑：「你是何人？」答曰：「吃素念佛。」王亦判云：「吃素念經，佛口蛇心，一百竹片，打斷脊筋。」尼哀告曰：「不瞞大王說，小婦人名雖是個尼姑，其實背地裡養漢，做私窠子的。」
stories.translation: A nun and a courtesan, upon death, appeared before Yangu. The King asked the courtesan, "What was your livelihood in your previous life?" The courtesan replied, "I kept men and entertained guests." The King judged, saying: "Keeping men and entertaining others, providing convenience for a solitary life. Send her back to the mortal world; let her be reborn soon." He asked the nun, "Who are you?" She replied, "I eat vegetarian food and recite sutras." The King also judged, saying: "Eating vegetarian and chanting scriptures, yet with a Buddha's mouth but a snake's heart. One hundred bamboo sticks, break the spinal sinews." The nun pleaded, saying: "I will not hide from Your Majesty. Though my name is a nun, in truth I secretly keep men and run an illicit brothel."

stories.text: 一學生聰穎，對答如流。師出兩字課曰：「月明。」徒即對曰：「日出。」又云：「和尚。」答曰：「尼姑。」師曰：「青山。」徒曰：「白水。」又出一字曰：「去。」徒即應聲曰：「來。」師又合串總念云：「月明和尚青山去。」徒亦答念對云：「日出尼姑白水來。」
stories.translation: A student was intelligent and fluent in his responses. The teacher gave a two-character lesson, saying: "Moon bright." The student immediately replied, "Sun rises." Then the teacher said: "Monk." The student replied, "Nun." The teacher said: "Green mountain." The student replied, "White water." Then the teacher gave a single character: "Go." The student immediately responded, saying, "Come." The teacher then recited the entire string together: "Moon bright monk green mountain go." The student also answered by reciting, "Sun rises nun white water come."

stories.text: 一尼到一施主人家化緣，暑天見主人睡在醉翁椅上，露出陽物甚偉。進對主家婆曰：「娘娘，你幾世上修來的，如此享用？」主婆曰：「阿彌陀佛，說這樣話。」尼曰：「這還說不修哩。」
stories.translation: A nun went to the house of a donor and begged for alms. On a hot summer day, she saw the master sleeping on a zuiweng chair with his large penis exposed. She then said to the master's wife, "Madam, how many lifetimes of cultivation did you have in order to enjoy such pleasures?" The mistress replied, "Amituofo, what words are these?" The nun said, "This is still considered not cultivated."
